note: A second, entirely separate Franceschi family — Venetian nobility settled at Imotski in inland Dalmatia — which a widely-copied online tree has been joined to the Crikvenica Defranceski by mistake. Reconstructed from the family's own MyHeritage GEDCOM of July 2018 and the local history site stariimotski.com.
why: This page exists because of an error, and the error is instructive. The family's MyHeritage tree — 8,286 individuals, 254 of them carrying this surname — descends the Crikvenica household from Zuane de Franceschi, a Venetian commander who was made governor of Imotski after the town was taken from the Ottomans in 1717. It is a magnificent pedigree and it is not ours. Setting out what the Imotski family actually is, and where the join was made, is worth more than quietly deleting it: the same tree has been copied outward through Geni and MyHeritage's Smart Matching since 2017, and anyone else who finds it will hit the same seam.

chain.what: The tree's earliest Dalmatian generation, at Zadar.
Married Maria Dešković. The by-name Perin is the one that sticks: the mills on the Vrljika that the family later held are still called Perinuša after their managers.
Married Lukrezia di Venezia de Franceschi.

The head of the Dalmatian house. Venetian commander at the taking of Imotski from the Ottomans in 1717, then governor of the town. The Republic rewarded him with large estates on the Vrljika, houses, a mill, and the tower of the arcibeg Čaušević at Perinuša.
Born at Omiš, died in the Proložac district. Married Francesca.
Born at Omiš. Married Contessa Maria Cambi.
Born at Omiš, died at Proložac. Married Katarina Dorić.

Landowner at Perinuša. Married in 1892 Ana pl. Grubišić of Omiš, born 19 September 1863, died 28 May 1936. Nine children. He rebuilt the house and the mills at Perinuša shortly before he died; a great lover of horses, he is said to have kept them overnight on the house terrace, up a laid ramp, out of the river damp.

children.what: Photographed in 1932 in one of the first motor cars in Imotski, waiting outside the elementary school at Poljica for his wife — Marija Dijaković of Dubrovnik, 1907–1953, a schoolteacher. Family tradition says he drove fast enough to reach Split in under three hours.

Born at Perinuša; the first trained seafarer from Imotski and its hinterland, and a ship's captain. In the summer of 1946, commanding the small steamer Hercegovina in the southern Adriatic, he came on a rowing boat that looked empty and was not: inside were a dead woman and a barely living man, Slovenes who had bought or stolen the boat at Dubrovnik and set out to row to Italy. Their baby had died first, then the wife. He fed the man, and telegraphed the parents to meet the ship at Rijeka. For years afterwards they came from Slovenia to thank him whenever the ship was in port, which annoyed him — he held that saving a man was a captain's plain duty — and he eventually asked the company to stop telling them which ship he was on.

Born at Perinuša. Educated at the lyceum of St Dimitrije in Zadar, the first private girls' high school for noble families, where the teaching was in Italian. A gifted painter all her life, in many techniques, and an embroiderer and designer. Buried at Gospa od Anđela, Imotski. Her photograph was taken at the Zita studio in Split in 1918.

Also at the Zadar lyceum. In the winter of 1925, coming home to Perinuša, the Vrljika was up and could only be crossed by cart; she would not wait for the driver and went barefoot through the cold water. The pneumonia that followed did not clear, and her mother sent her to the lung clinic at Davos in Switzerland — her brother Toni drove her. She died in September 1926, aged twenty-six. Four white horses drew her to the cemetery at Proložac.
Entered in the tree at Crikvenica, and photographed playing the accordion. One of the two individuals the tree places on both sides of the seam.

seam.heading: Where the two families were joined, and how to see it
seam.lead: The tree makes Anton Toni de Franceschi of Imotski, 1893–1941, the husband of Ursula Kovačina and the father of the Crikvenica children — Pepe, Zdravko, Ivan, Anka and Pero. He was neither.

points.lab: The tree records its own doubt in the names
points.text: Three of the four people at the seam are entered with question marks inside the name field: «Ursula Kovačina?», «Ana Nana Grubišić?», «Ana Kalaj-Kucarica ? (Kalanj??)». The compiler could not decide and wrote the uncertainty down. That is honest work, and it is the thread to pull.

points.lab: One woman is in the tree twice
points.text: Josip Bepo is given two wives. Ana Nana Grubišić, born 19 September 1863, died 28 May 1936. And Ana Kalaj-Kucarica ? (Kalanj??), born 1863, died 1936 at Crikvenica. Same birth year, same death year, no children on the second. They are one entry split in two — the Crikvenica Ana Kalanj and the Omiš Ana Grubišić, held apart by a question mark because the compiler suspected they were not the same and joined the families anyway.

points.lab: The dates make the marriage impossible
points.text: The Imotski account says Josip Bepo married Ana pl. Grubišić of Omiš in 1892. Our Ana Kalanj had already borne Anton Rudolf at Klenovica in January 1890 and Marija Stjepanka in December 1892. She cannot be a bride of 1892 at Omiš.

points.lab: The two Antons are two men
points.text: The Imotski Anton Toni was born in 1893 at Imotski and married Marija Dijaković of Dubrovnik, a schoolteacher, with whom he is photographed at Poljica in 1932. Our Anton Rudolf was born on 20 January 1890 at Klenovica house 22, baptised on 9 February, and married Ursula Kovačina. Three years and four hundred kilometres apart.

points.lab: The registers point the other way entirely
points.text: The Klenovica baptism of 1890 names the parents' place of origin as «Gallignana u Istriji» — Gračišće in Istria. The 1863 Gračišće baptism gives Josip's father Antonius as a lapicida, a stonecutter, and the 1906 death entry gives Josip himself as a «vešti klesar sada tvorničar». This is a family of stonemasons coming down off an Istrian hill, not Venetian landowners on the Vrljika.

seam.close: What the tree got right is that both families exist and both are well recorded. What it got wrong is the join — made, as these joins usually are, on a shared given name and a shared surname in a country where both are common. The Imotski Franceschi keep their governor. This archive keeps its stonemasons.

salvage.heading: What the tree gave that nothing else had
salvage.lead: Below the seam the same file is the best source this archive has for the Crikvenica generation — dates carried in the family's own knowledge, off gravestones and the backs of photographs, for people the registers here do not reach.

rows.what: Photographed on the pier at Crikvenica.
An accordion player. Placed by the tree among Josip Bepo's Imotski children, but born and working at Crikvenica — the second individual sitting across the seam.
Worked at Senj. Buried there — the family holds the gravestone photograph.
Ivan's wife, of the Blažević of Senj and Krmpote. She died in South Africa, six years to the day after her husband died in Senj.
The tree says 1999; two cemetery memorials at Horsham say December 1979. See below.
Zdravko's wife. Her Horsham memorial gives 1 February — the interment. Fužine confirms the Belnica origin the archive had from the displaced-persons papers.
Born in Germany to Zdravko and Ruža while they were there, and the exact date the Arolsen child-tracing papers were opened on. This is the single most valuable line in the file.
Anton Rudolf's wife and the mother of all of them. The tree gives her no dates, and neither does anything else this archive has found.

zdravko.heading: The 1999 that is not a death date
zdravko.text: The family's file and the MyHeritage tree both give Zdravko Defranceski's death as 1999 at Horsham. Two memorials in Horsham Cemetery give December 1979 — one reading «Zdravko "Frank" Defranceski, 1921 – 22 Dec 1979», the other, plot Central 2-J-10, entered under the garbled forename «Zorafko Frank De Franceski» and dated 27 December 1979. A death on the 22nd and an interment on the 27th is an ordinary week.
zdravko.how: The 1999 has a source, and the same file supplies it: his son Anton died on 28 June 1999 at Ipswich. A father's death year taken from the son's is one of the commonest slips in a compiled tree, and it is what happened here. Zdravko died in 1979, twenty years before the date the family has been carrying — and sixteen years before his wife Ruža, who outlived him and is buried in a different section of the same cemetery.

sourcing.detail: 8,286 individuals, 254 carrying the surname. Held by the family. Its Crikvenica and Blažević entries are first-hand; its Dalmatian and Venetian upper reaches are compiled from Geni Smart Matching in 2017 and carry no register citations.

A local history site for Imotski, cited in the tree's own notes as the origin of the Perinuša narratives — the mills, Mila's death, Captain Zane and the rowing boat. Credited there to the family archive of Captain Vjeko Franceschi.
